strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why adversarial training can retain good clean generalization while exhibiting a large robust train–test gap.

Separating transferable signal learning from sample-specific noise memorization offers an intuitive, potentially useful mechanism. Studying both representation complexity and training dynamics is well motivated.
The MNIST/CIFAR10 capacity sweeps document the motivating phenomenon, while synthetic feature trajectories and additional flatness experiments provide useful diagnostic observations.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider a balanced distribution on x = ±e₁ with corresponding labels, δ = 1/4, and f_clean(x) = x₁ + 8x₂. This satisfies Assumptions 4.1–4.3, but with N growing polynomially in D, both support points occur frequently in training. Vanishing robust training error then forces vanishing robust test error, making CGRO impossible. Additional assumptions controlling probability mass outside the memorized regions are necessary. Separately, Appendix F claims uniform o(1) approximation of a generally discontinuous indicator construction by continuous ReLU networks; this argument requires substantial correction.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish robust training error under the paper's definition. The training adversary in Section 5 can modify only the signal patch along w*, leaving the memorized noise patches untouched. Definition 3.3 instead maximizes over the entire perturbation ball. Small loss against the restricted adversary does not establish small full-ball robust training error, so the claimed CGRO conclusion does not follow.

The clean-generalization proof in Appendix E.12 contains essential mathematical gaps. It treats a cubic polynomial of Gaussian noise as sub-Gaussian, which is generally false, and does not control correlations between neurons evaluated on the same noise patches. It also infers a Θ(1) norm for every residual weight vector from aggregate training memorization scores, without justification. The resulting clean-test-error bound needs a valid concentration argument and explicit norm and width control.

The synthetic experiment does not satisfy the theorem's perturbation assumption: Section 6.2 sets δ = α = 10, whereas Assumption 5.7 requires δ < α. This permits complete erasure of the meaningful signal, so poor robust test performance can reflect removal of label information rather than the proposed learning mechanism. More broadly, PGD step sizes, iteration counts, restarts, and several optimization details are missing; repeated-run uncertainty and stronger attack checks are also absent. These omissions limit reproduction and confidence in the reported robustness.

The claimed lower-bound advance over Li et al. (2022) is unclear. Assumption 4.3 includes linearly separable distributions, and Appendix F again constructs a linearly separable hard distribution. Thus, the asserted extension needs a precise statement of what exceeds the previous result. Moreover, an existential worst-case lower bound does not establish the displayed complexity hierarchy for general distributions. The small MNIST models' collapse to constant predictions demonstrates a training outcome, not a representation lower bound.

The supplementary generalization bound in Theorem B.1 also fails as stated. An input-constant classifier has zero input-gradient term, yet its label-dependent empirical loss can fall below its population loss because sampled class proportions fluctuate. The asserted high-probability inequality therefore needs an additional sampling term or stronger assumptions. Appendix G also retains density-estimation bias and variance terms that disappear without justification from the final bound. Together with the central theorem issues, this leaves the principal theoretical contribution insufficiently supported for acceptance.
